target_customer: Pharmaceutical and biotech companies that want de novo designed antibody therapeutics for hard targets
problem: Finding antibodies that bind difficult targets at the right site, with good manufacturability and low toxicity, takes slow trial and error. Nabla pairs generative AI design with large scale wet lab testing.
business_model: Pharma partnerships with upfront and milestone payments plus royalties, plus services revenue
product_category: AI protein and antibody design for drug discovery

founders.name: Surge Biswas
education: PhD in George Church's lab at Harvard (YC page: recently completed)
founders.background_notes: YC page: 10 plus years using synthetic biology and machine learning. TechCrunch (Dec 2021) says he developed the core technology as a graduate student in the Church lab.

founders.name: Frances Anastassacos
prior_employers: Biotech venture capital (firm unnamed on YC page)
education: PhD in biological engineering at Harvard, class of 2019 BBS (YC page)
founders.background_notes: TechCrunch states she and Biswas are married.

founders.name: George Church
founders.background_notes: TechCrunch lists the Harvard professor as a co-founder; the YC page and the press release name only Biswas and Anastassacos.

competitors.name: Generate Biomedicines
competitors.what: Flagship Pioneering backed machine learning protein design company
competitors.traction_then: Emerged from stealth in September 2020 with evidence its platform designs proteins for multiple therapeutic uses
competitors.funding_then: Over 50 million dollars from Flagship at emergence

technical_complexity.rationale: De novo antibody design with generative models needs research-grade machine learning plus high throughput wet lab validation; the founders brought Harvard Church lab expertise.

defensibility.rationale: Proprietary experimental data and platform know-how are hard to copy, but well funded rivals like Generate were ahead on funding in 2021.

takeover_risk_then.outcome: Rather than buying or copying, three large pharmas (AstraZeneca, Bristol Myers Squibb, Takeda) signed collaborations with Nabla by May 2024.

market_need_then: Pharma had antibody targets that classical discovery struggled with; by Dec 2021 Nabla reported partnerships with five unnamed pharma companies, one grown into a multi-target collaboration.

branding.domain_note: Uses nabla.bio, a .bio domain; the AI clinical documentation firm Nabla uses a different domain.

identity.logo: Not confirmed by any source opened; the name matches the nabla math symbol, but no source says the company chose it for that
identity.voice_and_tone: Confident, mission driven and forward looking, for example Designing Better Medicines

brand_strength.rationale: Recognition comes from pharma partnerships and scientific publications rather than brand work; name is often confused with a clinical documentation company called Nabla.

outcome_analysis: Nabla grew from a Harvard Church lab spinout into an AI antibody design company with a seed of 11 million dollars in Dec 2021, pharma collaborations with AstraZeneca, Bristol Myers Squibb and Takeda worth over 550 million dollars in upfront and milestone payments, and a 26 million dollar Series A in May 2024. Strong founder market fit and a hard technical moat drove it; it remains active.
notes: Competitor entry for Generate Biomedicines is dated Sept 2020 from a BioCentury search result that I did not open; the 370M Series B (Nov 2021) is later and excluded. TechCrunch Dec 2021 also names Generate as the competitor. The Fifty Years led an earlier unannounced seed whose amount and date are not public, recorded with year 2021 as an approximation from the article, which only says earlier. Series A cross-checked by Pulse 2.0 and Pharma Letter in search results; total raised about 37M per the press release. Business Wire returned 403. Reports of a second Takeda deal worth over 1B are unverified. Aggregators list competitors Galux, Antiverse and others without dates.
